title: Of liars
paragraphs: There is no living man whom it would less become to speak from memory than me, for I have hardly any at all, and I do not think the world contains another so amazingly treacherous as mine. My other faculties are all sufficiently ordinary and middling; but in this one I think myself quite rare and singular, deserving to be famous for it. Beyond the natural inconvenience I suffer because of it (for, given how necessary the use of memory is, Plato was right to call it a great and powerful goddess), in my part of the country, when they want to say that a man has no sense, they say he has no memory; and when I complain that mine is defective, they do not believe me, and reprove me as though I were calling myself a fool — failing to see the difference between memory and understanding, which only makes things worse for me. But they do me wrong, for experience daily shows the opposite: that a strong memory is commonly paired with weak judgment. They also wrong me — me who am as perfect in nothing as in friendship — by making the very words that complain of my infirmity portray me as ungrateful. They draw my feelings into question on the basis of my memory, and from a natural imperfection make out a defect of conscience. "He has forgotten," says one, "this request, or that promise; he no longer remembers his friends; he has forgotten to say or do or hide this or that thing for my sake." And I am indeed apt to forget many things, but to neglect anything a friend has committed to my charge — that I never do. It ought to be enough that I feel the misery and inconvenience of it, without being branded with malice, a vice as contrary to my temper as anything could be.

Still, I take these comforts from my infirmity. First, that it is an evil from which I have chiefly found reason to correct a worse one that would easily have grown on me — namely, ambition, a fault that is intolerable in anyone taking on public affairs. As similar examples in the course of nature show, she has strengthened me in my other faculties in proportion as she has left me unfurnished in this one; otherwise I should have been apt to rest my mind and judgment, by default, on the bare reports of other men, never setting them to work on their own force, if the inventions and opinions of others had been continually available to me through the convenience of memory. By this means too I am not so talkative, for the storeroom of memory is always better stocked with material than the storeroom of invention. If mine had been faithful, I would by now have deafened all my friends with my chatter — the subjects rousing and stirring up the small faculty I have for handling and using them, warming and stretching out my discourse — which would be a pity, as I have observed in several of my close friends who, with their memories supplying them a complete and full view of things, begin their narrative so far back, and clutter it with so many irrelevant circumstances, that even when the story is a good one they manage to spoil it. If it is not a good one, you are left to curse either the strength of their memory or the weakness of their judgment. It is a hard thing to close off a discourse and cut it short once it is started; there is nothing in which the strength of a horse shows itself more than in a clean and sudden stop. I see even those who keep to the point, but cannot stop short in their career; for while they are casting about for a handsome cadence to finish with, they go on at random, wandering off into trivialities, like men staggering on weak legs. Above all, old men who keep the memory of things past, and forget how often they have told them, are dangerous company; I have known stories from the mouth of a man of very great quality, very pleasant in themselves, become wearisome by being repeated a hundred times over to the same people.

Secondly, this way I remember the injuries I have received less. As the ancient said, I should need a register of injuries, or a prompter, like Darius, who, so as not to forget the offence he had received from the people of Athens, had a page repeat in his ear three times every time he sat down to dinner: "Sir, remember the Athenians." And then again, the places I revisit, and the books I read over again, still smile on me with a fresh novelty.

It is not without good reason that it is said "that a man who has not a good memory should never take up the trade of lying." I know perfectly well that grammarians distinguish between speaking an untruth and lying, and say that to speak an untruth is to say something that is false but that we believe to be true, while the definition of the verb "to lie" in Latin (from which our French is taken) is to say something we know in our conscience to be untrue; and it is only this last sort of liar I am speaking of here. Now these either invent outright the untruths they tell, or alter and disguise a true story so completely that it ends in a lie. When they alter and disguise the same story to fit their own fancy, it is very hard for them, sooner or later, not to be tripped up; since the real truth of the matter, having taken first possession of the memory and lodged there through the channels of knowledge and study, will not easily refuse to present itself to the imagination and crowd out the falsehood, which cannot have so sure and settled a footing there as the other; and the circumstances of the first, true knowledge, always running in their minds, will make them forget those that are illegitimate and forged by their own fancy. When they wholly invent, since there is no contrary impression to push against their invention, there seems to be less danger of stumbling — and yet even this, because it is an empty body without anything to anchor it, is very apt to escape the memory if it is not very firmly fixed. I have had very entertaining experience of this at the expense of men who make a business of fitting their speech to the affair they have in hand, or to the humour of the great folk they are addressing; for the circumstances to which these men readily enslave their good faith and conscience being subject to several changes, their language has to vary accordingly. So it happens that of the same thing they tell one man it is this, and another that it is that, giving it different colours — and these men, if they ever happen to compare notes and discover the trick, what becomes of this fine art? To which one should add that they must, of necessity, very often ridiculously trip themselves up; for what memory could possibly retain so many different shapes as they have forged about one and the same subject? I have known many in my time very ambitious of the reputation for this sort of cleverness, but they do not see that if they get the reputation, the effect can no longer follow.

In plain truth, lying is an accursed vice. We are men, and we have no tie on one another except by our word. If we really understood the horror and gravity of it, we should pursue lying with fire and sword, and more justly than other crimes. I see that parents commonly, and rather unwisely, correct their children for little innocent faults, and torment them over trifles that leave no impression and have no consequence; whereas, in my opinion, lying, and at a lower level, obstinacy, are the faults that should be severely thrashed out of them, both in their infancy and as they grow. Otherwise they grow up and grow worse with them, and once a tongue has got the trick of lying, it is unimaginable how impossible it is to reclaim. Hence we see some men, otherwise quite honest, so subject and enslaved to this vice. I have an honest lad for my tailor whom I have never once known to tell a truth, not even when it would have been to his advantage. If falsehood, like truth, had only one face, we should be on better terms with it, for we should then take for certain the opposite of whatever the liar said. But the reverse of truth has a hundred thousand faces and a boundless field, without limit. The Pythagoreans hold that good is certain and finite, and evil infinite and uncertain. There are a thousand ways to miss the mark; there is only one way to hit it. For my own part, I have such a horror of this vice that I am not sure I could prevail on my conscience to save myself from the most evident and extreme danger by a blatant and solemn lie. An ancient father says that "a dog we know is better company than a man whose language we do not understand."
"Ut externus alieno pene non sit hominis vice."
["So that a foreigner is almost not a man at all to us." — Pliny, Natural History, vii. 1.]
And how much less sociable is false speech than silence?

King Francis I boasted that he had by this means tied up Francesco Taverna, the ambassador of Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan — a man very famous in his day for his skill in talking. This gentleman had been sent to excuse his master to His Majesty in a very serious business, which was this: the king, in order to keep up some intelligence in Italy, out of which he had lately been driven, and particularly with the Duchy of Milan, had thought it convenient to keep a gentleman of his own on hand with the duke — an ambassador in effect, but in outward appearance a private person who was supposed to be residing there on his own affairs. The duke, being much more dependent on the emperor (especially while he was negotiating his marriage with the emperor's niece, daughter of the King of Denmark, who is now the dowager of Lorraine), could not show any open dealings or conferences with us without serious risk. For this commission, one Merveille, a Milanese gentleman and an equerry of the king, was thought very suitable, and was sent there with private credentials and instructions as ambassador, along with other letters of recommendation to the duke concerning his own private affairs, the better to mask and colour the business. He was so long at that court that the emperor at last got wind of his real employment there — which was the cause, we suppose, of what followed: under pretext of some murder, his trial was dispatched in two days, and his head was struck off in prison at night. Messire Francesco arrived in France prepared with a long counterfeit account of the affair (for the king had applied to all the princes of Christendom, as well as to the duke himself, to demand satisfaction) and was given his audience at the morning council. There, after he had laid out several plausible justifications of the fact in support of his case — that his master had never looked on Merveille as anything but a private gentleman and his own subject, who was there only on his own business, and had never lived under any other character; absolutely denying that he had ever heard he was a member of the king's household, or that His Majesty so much as knew him, so far was he from taking him for an ambassador — the king, pressing him in turn with several objections and demands and challenging him from every side, tripped him up at last by asking, then, why the execution had been carried out at night, and as it were by stealth. At which the poor confounded ambassador, the more elegantly to extricate himself, replied that the duke would have been very loath, out of respect for His Majesty, to have such an execution carried out by day. One can imagine how he was scolded when he got home, for having so grossly tripped in the presence of a prince of so delicate a nose as King Francis.

Pope Julius II, having sent an ambassador to the King of England to stir him up against King Francis, had his ambassador heard. Before he would give an answer, the king urged the difficulties he would meet in setting on foot so great a preparation as would be needed to attack so powerful a king, and gave his reasons. The ambassador very unseasonably replied that he too had considered the same difficulties and had laid them before the pope. From this saying, so directly contrary to the matter in hand and the business he had come for (which was simply to incite the king to war), the King of England first drew the conclusion (which he later found to be true) that this ambassador, in his own heart, was on the French side. He notified the pope, the ambassador's estate was confiscated at his return, and he himself only narrowly escaped losing his head.
